In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of laser spectroscopic techniques for the study of cardiovascular tissue and the use of these techniques to characterize the tissue and its response to laser irradiation.
the development of laser spectroscopy as an analytical technique to study cardiovascular tissue.
developing an understanding of the spectroscopic characteristics of cardiovascular tissue and the mechanisms by which laser radiation interacts with this tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results obtained are not sufficient to support or refute the hypothesis that laser light can be used to remove atheromatous material.
the spectroscopic data are consistent with the presence of collagen and elastin, but not of cholesterol or calcium, in atherosclerotic plaques.

the spectroscopic data obtained are not sufficient to make a final judgment on the feasibility of laser angioplastics, but rather that the spectroscopic results are encouraging and should be pursued further.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spectroscopic methods used are sensitive to the molecular structure of cardiovascular tissue.
the spectroscopic measurements of cardiovascular tissue are consistent with the hypothesis that the laser-induced thermal damage is the major factor in laser angioplasty.
the laser spectroscopic techniques used in this study are capable of providing a detailed chemical analysis of in vitro cardiovascular tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
laser angioplasty is a complex procedure, and that a better understanding of the underlying tissue chemistry is necessary to improve the safety and efficacy of the procedure.
spectroscopy is an important tool for characterizing the structure of biological tissue and can provide useful information for laser tissue interactions.
